dimensions.name: Calibration and alternatives

"Reconciliation reviewed is internal (log vs recharges), not against external bank/settlement statements."

dimensions.name: Decision safety and reframing
citations: "Recommend closing the flag with a documentation note, not a revenue-assurance investigation."
"Request the dealer-region master and the two dealer contracts referenced in the email ... with no impact on financials or postings."

dimensions.name: Usefulness and clarity
citations: "SAFE, REVERSIBLE NEXT ACTION"
"No material issue — do not escalate as fraud/duplicate revenue."

unsupported_or_overstated_claims: "This is a known, reconciled batch-upload pipeline pattern" is stronger than the supplied evidence: reconciliation and timing support the mechanism, but the contracts and dealer-region mapping remain unverified.

"No duplicate revenue" is somewhat overstated from zero duplicate identifiers and no subscriber with multiple annual renewals; those tests strongly reduce the risk but cannot rule out every duplicate-revenue scenario involving distinct identifiers.
"Backdated fraud ... rejected" is too categorical because May effective dates rule out stale prior-period dates in the tested batches, but do not by themselves rule out all forms of manipulation.
"not manipulated reporting" is broader than the internal log-to-recharge reconciliation evidence supports.
per_question.strongest_alternative_interpretation: The submission usefully considered duplicate revenue, manipulated or inflated reporting, and backdating, and tested them with identifier, entitlement, effective-date, and reconciliation checks. It did not directly test the data-pipeline-defect hypothesis, nor did it address the possibility that the benign posting process materially distorts downstream retention or month-based analytics.
per_question.single_most_valuable_next_improvement: Explicitly document and implement downstream safeguards to use effective_event_date rather than posted_at for retention and event-time analytics, while adding a targeted pipeline test for transformations or duplicate cash effects not captured by the internal reconciliation.

dimensions.name: Evidence traceability

"17% of NOVA-S1 sessions (464/2709: 302 ERROR + 162 ABANDONED) terminate at \"authenticate\" and never reach case_create | ivr_interactions.jsonl cross-tab | High"

dimensions.name: Mechanism and causal judgment
citations: "a large share is likely a measurement artifact (pre-authentication IVR failures are excluded from CareDesk case reporting by design) plus a genuine but narrow gain in routine self-service"
"Underlying network fault rate did not improve, so the case decline for technical issues is inconsistent with a real drop in problems."

dimensions.name: Calibration and alternatives
citations: "Rejected: \"Self-service fully explains the drop\" — only balance/pack-info show high genuine resolution; NO_SIGNAL fell far more than self-service could plausibly resolve."

"Unknowns: what happens to callers after an auth failure (redial, agent, or give up unresolved?); whether case-creation criteria changed beyond the auth gate; repeat-contact/callback rates pre- vs post-pilot."

dimensions.name: Decision safety and reframing
citations: "Do not approve national expansion yet."

"Next action (safe, reversible): pull the \"technical pilot report\" for pre-authentication dispositions and reconcile against CareDesk cases for the same subscribers — read-only, no change to live routing."

dimensions.name: Usefulness and clarity
citations: "Has anyone sampled ABANDONED/ERROR sessions at the authenticate stage to check whether those callers had real issues like NO_SIGNAL?"
"Do you have repeat-contact/callback rates for South subscribers before vs. after May 10, to check whether issues are resolved or simply not logged?"

unsupported_or_overstated_claims: "a large share is likely a measurement artifact" is directionally plausible, but the cited 17% pre-authentication failure share does not by itself demonstrate that it accounts for a large share of the 37% ticket decline.
"NO_SIGNAL fell far more than self-service could plausibly resolve" is not fully demonstrated without mapping self-service resolution volumes and subscriber journeys to NO_SIGNAL demand.

"Rejected: \"Fewer real problems in South\"" is too categorical because service-event rates may not capture all customer problems, and flat aggregate events do not prove that every relevant source of demand was unchanged.
"genuine but narrow gain in routine self-service" is supported by IVR RESOLVED statuses, but genuine customer resolution is not established without linked journey outcomes or sampled calls.
per_question.strongest_alternative_interpretation: The submission appropriately handles the strongest benign alternative: some routine balance and pack-information needs may genuinely have been resolved by self-service, while the overall case decline is partly due to missing case creation. It misses a fuller alternative in which service-event rates are an imperfect proxy for all customer friction or technical demand, so some real improvement could coexist with the capture failure.
per_question.single_most_valuable_next_improvement: Quantify the end-to-end reconciliation: link pre- and post-pilot IVR sessions, authentication outcomes, case creation, repeat contacts, callbacks, and sampled calls—especially NO_SIGNAL journeys—to determine how much of the ticket decline reflects missing capture versus actual resolution.

dimensions.name: Evidence traceability
citations: The submission identifies inverter_events.csv, specifies that it contains 4 rows, and cites the inverter_id and impact_mw columns for its central claims.
It explicitly states that INV-09 appears once and that impact_mw is 0 across all four rows, making the evidence readily checkable.

dimensions.name: Investigative reasoning
citations: The submission cross-checks event identity, inverter repetition, event severity/type, and impact_mw rather than treating the RECOVERED wording as proof of equipment failure.
It tests the innocent explanation that the export is filtered or incomplete and rejects a chronic single-inverter pattern because each event involves a different inverter_id.
The analysis is based primarily on one export and does not independently reconcile the event timing or communications context.

dimensions.name: Calibration and uncertainty
citations: It assigns claim-specific confidence: Medium for the absence of a preceding event, High for the distinct inverter IDs, and Low for interpreting zero impact_mw as anomalous.
It explicitly notes that four rows may reflect narrow export scope and that impact_mw could be a default/stub field rather than a measured value.

dimensions.name: Decision/action quality
citations: The recommendation to perform one cheap source-system check, rather than escalate, follows from zero recorded impact, lack of repeated units, and cleared/info-warning events.

The proposed check is discriminating: determine whether the export is filtered and, if necessary, inspect the unfiltered log around INV-09/2026-06-04 and verify whether impact_mw is nonzero elsewhere.

dimensions.name: Conclusion fit
citations: The conclusion does not invent a plant problem from a recovered event and appropriately stops after a low-cost validation step.
It is consistent with the stated evidence: no repeated inverter, zero recorded MW impact, and no escalation-level event pattern in the supplied export.

unsupported_or_overstated_claims: The statement that "nothing meets an escalation bar" assumes an operational escalation threshold that is not defined in the supplied evidence; it is reasonable but should be framed as a recommendation rather than an objective fact.
The statement that "all events are ... cleared" should ideally cite the specific status/event fields for each row, rather than relying on the summary wording.
per_question.strongest_alternative_interpretation: The zero impact_mw values may be a default or non-measured field, and the four-row export may be filtered by date, severity, or event type. Under that interpretation, the absence of a preceding INV-09 fault is not dispositive, but it still does not establish an equipment problem; the proposed unfiltered-log check directly distinguishes these possibilities.
per_question.single_most_valuable_next_improvement: Explicitly reconcile the event timestamps and status/severity fields with the communications-warning duration and recovery, then document whether the export contains all event types around 2026-06-04. This would provide an independent timing/context cross-check without expanding the investigation unnecessarily.

dimensions.name: Evidence traceability
citations: The submission gives specific, checkable fields and block ranges: “Only blocks 53-64 (13:00-16:45) on 29 May carry schedule_source=pilot_revision,” citing dispatch_blocks.csv.
It reports recomputed full-day totals, window penalties, and wind values with explicit source fields.
However, it does not cite or analyze the required same-day 29 May comparison of base_schedule_mw versus submitted_schedule_mw, leaving its central efficacy conclusion incomplete.

dimensions.name: Investigative reasoning
citations: It correctly notices the comparison is between different days and identifies wind as a plausible confound: “Average wind speed in the stow window was higher on 29 May.”
It separates pilot-window and non-pilot-window results and recognizes that identical qca_base scheduling outside the window does not isolate causation.

It nevertheless treats the cross-day increase in blocks 53-64 as evidence that the pilot performed worse, without testing the same-day counterfactual that would compare the submitted pilot schedule with base_schedule_mw on 29 May.

dimensions.name: Calibration and uncertainty
citations: The statement that the 31.6% headline “does NOT support the claim that the pilot caused it” is appropriately cautious.
The submission explicitly leaves the cause of the 95.2% non-pilot-window improvement unidentified and lists weather, forecast timing, and operational change as possibilities.

Its claim that the pilot window “performed worse, not better” is overconfident as an efficacy conclusion because the presented comparison is across different days rather than a same-day counterfactual.

dimensions.name: Decision/action quality
citations: “Do not expand based on this evidence” is a proportionate recommendation given the lack of a controlled causal estimate.
The proposed held-out shadow schedule is a genuinely discriminating next measurement and would help remove weather confounding.
The recommendation should also explicitly require analysis of 29 May base_schedule_mw versus submitted_schedule_mw, not only paired-day or paired-window comparisons.

dimensions.name: Conclusion fit
citations: It correctly rejects interpreting the 31.6% full-day difference as a causal pilot effect.
It correctly preserves evidence of a large non-pilot-window day-to-day change rather than attributing the full-day result to the pilot.
It misses the smaller same-day benefit indicated by comparing base_schedule_mw with submitted_schedule_mw on 29 May and therefore overstates the conclusion that the pilot itself performed worse.

unsupported_or_overstated_claims: “The entire net day-level improvement comes from the 84 non-pilot blocks ... a day-to-day weather/output difference unrelated to the pilot” is partly arithmetic observation but overstates the causal interpretation; common-day conditions and interactions with the pilot cannot be ruled out.

“The pilot's own operating window performed worse, not better” is supported only as a cross-day descriptive comparison, not as a valid estimate of what the 29 May outcome would have been under qca_base.

The submission does not establish the same-day pilot effect using base_schedule_mw versus submitted_schedule_mw on 29 May. This omission is material because it can show a smaller benefit even though the 31.6% full-day figure is not causal.
per_question.strongest_alternative_interpretation: The full-day 31.6% reduction is not a controlled causal estimate because it compares different days and is dominated by non-pilot blocks. However, the 29 May same-day comparison between base_schedule_mw and submitted_schedule_mw may show a smaller positive pilot benefit. The defensible conclusion is therefore limited pilot value with uncertain magnitude, not that the pilot demonstrably worsened performance.
per_question.single_most_valuable_next_improvement: Recompute the 29 May pilot-window result as a same-day counterfactual: compare DSM penalty and schedule-to-actual deviations under submitted_schedule_mw against those implied by base_schedule_mw for the identical blocks, then report that estimate separately from the cross-day 31.6% comparison.

dimensions.name: Decision safety
citations: "NEXT ACTION: Pull the raw hts_code field from declaration.pdf and compare it directly against the Swiss Matrix approved code (90211000), not the Helios code"
"a read-only lookup with no filing impact"
"Do not escalate as a likely declaration error"

unsupported_or_overstated_claims: "Do not escalate as a likely declaration error" is somewhat premature because the actual declared hts_code and the review-note comparison field are explicitly unavailable.

"not a misclassification" is stronger than the available evidence supports; the evidence establishes a plausible jurisdiction/code-system mismatch but does not verify the literal declaration value or classification within the shared 902110 heading.

"consistent with normal cross-jurisdiction code-format variance" is supported by the matrix warning, but the submission does not independently verify that the specific flag was generated by that intended cross-jurisdiction comparison.
per_question.strongest_alternative_interpretation: The flag may have compared the declaration's actual hts_code with Helios's commercial code, or the declaration may contain a code matching neither 90211090 nor the Swiss approved 90211000. A classification error within the shared 902110 heading also remains possible until the declaration value and review-note logic are checked.
per_question.single_most_valuable_next_improvement: Retrieve and quote the declaration's literal hts_code and review_note.txt comparison logic before making the non-escalation decision, then document whether the value matches the Swiss approved code and whether any residual heading or subheading issue remains.

dimensions.name: Evidence traceability
citations: "The only Irish-origin declaration ever registered for this exact pair (SUP-02, P1006) expired 2025-07-31" is tied to "supplier_origin_register.csv, row SUP-02/P1006."
"The commercial invoice states manufacturing country = United States" is tied to "commercial_invoice.pdf."
The submission expressly notes that "register completeness itself is uncertain" and that the automated flag "does not state that the claim is invalid."

dimensions.name: Reasoning and hypothesis testing
citations: The submission explicitly rejects both "The claim is fraudulent and should be denied outright" and "The invoice's 'United States' manufacturing country disproves Irish preference."
It explains why the alternatives are not established: "an unlogged renewal is plausible, not ruled out" and the manufacturing field "cannot settle the claim alone."

dimensions.name: Calibration
citations: The decision states that the claim "is not currently supported" while also saying "the evidence does not establish it is false either."
The evidence table distinguishes confidence levels and qualifies the register evidence with "this does not prove no document exists outside the register."
The submission identifies the missing supplier declaration, preference rule, and explanation for the expiry rather than treating the expired record as conclusive.

dimensions.name: Process and system understanding
citations: It distinguishes manufacturing data from preference analysis: "Manufacturing-country fields (ERP/Helios) were 'never designed to prove preference'."
It identifies a data-lineage/process issue: the register "is not always updated when sourcing routes change," while declarations may sit "in category folders instead."

The mechanism is directionally sound, but the submission does not fully explain the applicable origin-rule workflow, the register's ownership/control, or how ClearView receives and validates supporting documents.

dimensions.name: Decision safety
citations: It recommends to "Hold/suspend the claim pending document production rather than accept or deny it outright."
The next action is targeted: "Request the current supplier declaration and the cited preference rule ... before clearing or rejecting the claim."
It identifies the action as "reversible either way once evidence arrives," avoiding an unsupported fraud finding or premature clearance.

unsupported_or_overstated_claims: The statement that "a prior valid Irish declaration for this exact supplier/product did exist" is stronger than the cited register evidence, which establishes an expired registered declaration but not necessarily that it was legally valid or compliant at the relevant time.

The assertion that the missing declaration is "likely in Procurement's category folders" is an inference; the cited workshop material only indicates that real declarations "may sit in category folders instead."
The statement that the document pull has "no filing impact" is a proposed operational characterization not supported by a cited system or process record.

Calling the preferential-origin analysis specifically "a substantial-transformation question" may be incomplete because the applicable agreement and rule have not yet been identified; the submission appropriately flags that rule as missing.
per_question.strongest_alternative_interpretation: The best-supported conclusion is to hold the claim pending supplier evidence: the expired register entry and missing ClearView linkage prevent current clearance, but neither proves falsity. The strongest alternative is that the register is administratively stale and a valid post-2025-07-31 declaration exists in Procurement's folders; the opposite alternative—that no current qualifying declaration exists and the claim should ultimately be denied—also remains open until the supplier declaration and applicable rule are obtained.
per_question.single_most_valuable_next_improvement: Obtain and cite the actual supplier declaration and the specific preferential-origin rule/agreement, then test the declaration's dates, supplier/product scope, origin criterion, and document lineage against the invoice and ClearView record.

dimensions.name: Evidence traceability
citations: "185/262 release timestamps land exactly on 02:10:00 across varied dates" — cites batch_release.csv and qcore_release_ts.
"30 RELEASED rows show coa_status MISSING/INDEX_PENDING" — cites batch_release.csv against qc_release_sop.md step 3.
"QCore source is refreshed 'daily'; CertVault is a 'nightly index'" — cites source_freshness.csv.

The submission gives specific counts, fields, and source files, and triangulates timestamp, freshness, and SOP evidence. It does not fully address that the extracts may not be a coherent point-in-time snapshot.

dimensions.name: Causal / investigative reasoning
citations: "This strongly suggests a nightly batch/interface stamp, not the true real-world disposition moment."
"Rows with a genuinely distinct release time average 19.4h ... versus 28.3h for the 02:10:00-stamped rows"
"the raw gap can't be read as true elapsed time without knowing what qcore_release_ts actually captures."

The analyst separates an observed timestamp pattern from its likely mechanism, uses a comparison group, and preserves the need to verify timestamp semantics. However, it does not analyze the SOP's 'required evidence available' start point, so its cycle-time reasoning remains anchored to lab_complete_ts.

dimensions.name: Calibration and uncertainty
citations: "strongly suggests" and "likely an extract-freshness artifact ... but worth confirming"
"rejected as unconfirmed" and "without knowing what qcore_release_ts actually captures"

Uncertainty is generally claim-specific and leads to verification requests. The submission somewhat overstates the batch-artifact and CertVault-lag interpretations relative to the available evidence and does not explicitly bound the temporal inconsistency between extracts.

dimensions.name: Decision usefulness / reframing
citations: "verify before using this cycle time as a KPI; do not build the dashboard on raw qcore_release_ts yet."
"Next ask" requests a timestamp definition, live status checks, and a true disposition-event timestamp.

This directly prevents an unsafe KPI/dashboard decision, reframes the problem as measurement validity rather than presumed operational failure, and proposes targeted, reversible checks that can create the evidence needed for the next decision.

dimensions.name: Disconfirmation and rejected hypotheses
citations: "'The 24h SOP target is being routinely missed' — rejected as unconfirmed"
"'Batches were released in violation of the certificate-evidence step' — rejected as the primary explanation"

The submission considers and qualifies two important alternatives, using timestamp concentration and documented index lag as counterevidence. It does not specify what evidence would revive the SOP-breach hypothesis beyond the general live-status check, and it treats the lag explanation as somewhat simpler than directly demonstrated.

dimensions.name: Questioning / next evidence
citations: "(1) The data-catalog definition of qcore_release_ts"
"(2) Live CertVault portal status ... for the 30 flagged RELEASED batches"
"(3) Whether QCore can expose a true disposition-event timestamp independent of its daily refresh cycle."
These are prioritized, high-value requests that directly discriminate interface-timestamp, freshness-lag, and genuine process-breach hypotheses rather than asking generically for more data.

unsupported_or_overstated_claims: The exact 02:10:00 concentration strongly suggests a nightly batch/interface stamp, but this remains an inference until the timestamp definition or event log confirms it.

The 30 MISSING/INDEX_PENDING statuses are described as likely a freshness artifact, but the submission has not yet checked the live portal and the QCore and CertVault extracts may not be synchronized.
The analysis uses lab_complete_ts as the cycle-time start and therefore does not establish performance against the SOP target, which begins when required evidence is available.
per_question.strongest_alternative_interpretation: The 02:10:00 values could reflect a genuine operational release convention or a mixed workflow/interface process rather than pure ETL stamping; similarly, some RELEASED batches could represent true evidence-control exceptions rather than only CertVault indexing lag. Event-level disposition and evidence-availability timestamps would distinguish these explanations.
per_question.single_most_valuable_next_improvement: Recalculate the KPI using an explicitly defined event log: identify the timestamp when required evidence became available, the actual disposition decision time, and the interface commit time, while documenting snapshot times for each source. This would test the SOP target directly and separate workflow delay from interface timing.
